title: Why Ordinary Let Cannot Define a Recursive Closure
description: See why evaluating a recursive function inside a standard Let expression fails when the function body tries to look up its own name.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Lines 4-19 add `Mul` and `If0` (`test == 0`) to the AST dataclasses, and lines 21-36 define `Env` and `Closure(param, body, env)`.
In `interp(e, env)`, look at `Let` on lines 46-48. Line 47 evaluates `v = interp(e.val, env)` in the outer `env` first. Only afterward does line 48 call `env.extend(e.name, v)` to evaluate `e.body`.

Trace lines 45-48 when `e.val` is `Fun`: line 47 runs `Closure(e.param, e.body, env)` using the outer `env` (which does not yet contain `e.name`). When `Call` runs on line 51, `fn.body` runs in `fn.env.extend(fn.param, arg)`, whose parent chain is that outer `env`.
Lines 55-58 build `program = Let("fact", Fun("n", fact_body), Call(Var("fact"), Num(5)))`, where `fact_body` calls `Var("fact")` when `n` is non-zero.

steps.question: When `interp(program, Env())` runs on line 61, the outer `Call(Var("fact"), Num(5))` finds `"fact"` in the `Let` body's extended environment. What happens inside `fact_body` on line 57 when it evaluates `Var("fact")`?
steps.answer: Inside `fact_body`, the environment is `fn.env.extend("n", 5)`. Here, `fn.env` is the empty `Env()` captured before `"fact"` was bound, so `env.lookup("fact")` raises `NameError: undefined: 'fact'`.

steps.description: Lines 67-79 outline the three follow-up exercises on cyclic closure environments (`letrec` and tying the knot).
Line 45 builds `Closure('n', fact_body, env)` while `env.bindings` is still `{}` (before `Let` extends `env` with `'fact'`).
